title_en: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping Commits the Cardinal Sin of Prequels
summary_en: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping ending explained: We take a look at the latest entry in the franchise and examine the cardinal sin of prequels.
body_en:
Spoilers for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping follow.
When we first meet him in The Hunger Games, Haymitch Abernathy (originally portrayed by Woody Harrelson) is a broken, bitter, cynical alcoholic deeply uninterested in — or perhaps incapable of — helping Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson) survive the Games: his one job. Throughout the four original films, he transforms into a man who is not only trustworthy but who plays an integral role in the plan to finally, definitively, take down the Capitol. It’s one of the more powerful arcs in the series, one that speaks to the power of Katniss’ ability — mostly unwillingly and unwittingly —to inspire hope. The end of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the beginning of the Haymitch we have known; the issue is that the additions in this new film detract from the character rather than enrich him.
While the Haymitch of Sunrise on the Reaping (beautifully portrayed by Joseph Zada) is technically victorious in his Games, he has brutally lost to the Capitol and President Snow (Ralph Fiennes). As Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin) reviews Haymitch’s gameplay for a (presumably) Panem-wide audience, it is clear that the Gamemakers have edited Haymitch’s footage to show him in the worst possible light. From the Capitol’s perspective, he’s an ideal victor: unfeeling, ruthless, self-serving, cowardly, and lacking regard for the other tributes. This image of Haymitch is designed by the Capitol to serve its purpose; to make people selfish is to keep them separate and incapable of effectively challenging power. The intent is to send Haymitch home a pariah rather than a conquering hero who inspires others in 12 to reach beyond their current position. It also plays on his very real shame for failing to “break the Games,” which — as the Capitol did in the arena — forces him into isolation. Manipulating the footage is a tactic that, as we’ll get to, creates a real problem for the original films.
When Haymitch returns to 12, the Capitol has timed it so that he arrives just in time to watch his family burn alive in their small home, but too late to save them. With added cruelty, Snow allows him to briefly believe that the love of his life, Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak), will be spared, only for her to die from Snow’s poison, hidden in what looks like the candy Haymitch so lovingly gave her at the start of the film. The metaphor is clear: All the sweetness in his life has been irrevocably poisoned. He is left terrified that the Capitol will murder anyone he is close to, so he keeps everyone at bay. Early in the film, Haymitch made it clear he wanted no part of winning, or the lonely, traumatized, lifeless survival it would mean; Snow’s ultimate punishment is forcing him to live exactly that fate.
Snow, however, was manipulated into sparing Haymitch by Jesse Plemons’ Plutarch Heavensbee, who is playing the looooong game and wants to keep Haymitch around as a potential ally to one day end the Capitol’s authoritarian reign of terror. Plutarch knew Haymitch’s loved ones would likely be taken from him; he suggested as much. But he valued a future strategic alliance more than Haymitch’s peace. (With friends like these…) Ultimately, the Games portrayed in this film act as a dress rehearsal for Catching Fire’s conspiracy to “break the Games,” which is in part the issue with this story; more on that in a bit.
In a final montage, we hear young Haymitch in voice-over, vowing to keep his promise to two women who helped draw out his spirit of rebellion. The first is Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), one of District 12’s two female tributes. She’s basically a walking middle finger to the Games and the Capitol. The second is his murdered love, Lenore, who introduced the film’s central recurring theme, “nothing is inevitable,” meaning don’t submit to a fate you don’t want just because the current system wants you to believe there’s nothing you can do about it.
As images of Haymitch — angry, drunk, alone, and at odds with the community (in one shot, he is literally walking in the opposite direction) — play out on screen, he swears to be a terrible victor, to be disruptive, and presumably to eventually do what he set out to do in this film: end the Games. After being the teetotaling light of the community earlier in the film, he has become the Haymitch we know, even lurking behind a tree as his former friends cradle their new baby girl, little Katniss Everdeen. Throughout the series of images, he stands grimly before caskets as body after body is sent back to 12 from the Games. Believing he is too dangerous to be around, he lets no one comfort him.
The film concludes with a very brief flash-forward in which Lawrence, Hutcherson, and Harrelson return as the grown Katniss, Peeta, and an older Haymitch, celebrating that there is no more Reaping (which had taken place each year on Haymitch’s birthday). They thank one another for what they each did to end the bloodshed; then Haymitch goes to sit on the hill where he once found refuge with Lenore.
One is led to believe that Haymitch is at peace. Lenore promised that change is possible, and Plutarch assured Haymitch that each act of rebellion adds a spark that may lead to the next, and that even if they never see the results in their lifetime, the effort is worth it. But the conclusion of Sunrise on the Reaping shows a man who did see his work pay off in his own lifetime. His goal had been to end the Games, he sacrificed everything for it, and eventually, he got what he wanted — he kept his promise. And therein lies the problem: Turning the original Hunger Games story into the fulfillment of Haymitch’s long-delayed goal undercuts the power of those first films.
The question isn’t whether this is a faithful adaptation of Suzanne Collins’ book, but whether it supports or undercuts the world the original films created. There are aspects of this movie that work; Zada, as mentioned, is a standout. However, a prequel’s one job is to deepen the original, and this one weakens it. The voice-over itself encapsulates the core issue with the story: It tells us who Haymitch becomes and why. According to Sunrise on the Reaping, Haymitch didn’t evolve into a man capable of playing a key role in a revolution — he’d been lying in wait the whole time. Here’s what gets lost: If the hope and intention were always there, then the transformation we thought we witnessed wasn’t real, and suddenly one of the franchise’s best character journeys loses its meaning.
In Catching Fire, Harrelson’s Haymitch tells Katniss, “Nobody ever wins the Games. Period. There are survivors. There’s no winners.” That sentiment carries multiple meanings. The Games are designed to exacerbate individual and collective trauma: You must scrape, fight, and kill to survive, and the person in front of you is never your real enemy, just another lost soul. Even if you “win,” you’ve lost something essential in yourself; you’ve become a cog in that machine — an instrument of death and cruelty, a weapon for a system that would just as soon grind you to a pulp.
In Sunrise on the Reaping, Haymitch’s failure is a narrow one. He actually does destroy a large part of the arena, but the Capitol manipulates the footage so no one knows. He fails to blow up the Games publicly, which is far less complex than a true moral failing — winning because he did play the game and played it well. Here, he is almost angelically good: rebellious, self-sacrificing, and when he kills, it’s by accident or in self-defense. That unimpeachable sense of honor is less potent and relatable than a character who, despite their best intentions, gets caught up in something they can’t navigate with their morals intact.
Harrelson’s Haymitch felt like someone who had failed — not in a worthy attempt, but by failing himself. The kids are on their own in there; that’s the horror of it. It’s human to betray our own values out of fear, to become the very thing we’d hate to be. And an institution like the Capitol relies on exactly that — on our fear, our compliance, and the debilitating shame of our choice to comply. The original Haymitch suggests someone who did what he had to in order to survive, then spent decades carrying that shame until he was finally given a chance at redemption. That’s a kind of grace, and a far more interesting character. This Haymitch, by contrast, had a conspiracy behind him. His failure is that it didn’t work, and kids died anyway.
This movie also makes the events of Catching Fire far too neat. It now feels like a very convenient “getting the gang back together,” with Beetee, Wiress, and Plutarch all called into play by circumstances no one could have foreseen (such as the death of Gamemaker Seneca Crane). As for Plutarch, Philip Seymour Hoffman’s portrayal of a new Head Gamemaker who turns out to be a rebel insider was rich and complex. One got the sense that he had, over time, allowed the horror of what he was doing (finding ever more creative ways to get kids to kill each other) to slowly seep into his consciousness. According to Sunrise on the Reaping, Plutarch has been a rebel from the start, spending decades rising through the Capitol’s ranks just in case he ever found a new moment to act. That’s a long time to slaughter children before taking a stand.
Removing the emotional impact of key characters is one of the cardinal sins of a prequel, but Sunrise on the Reaping also introduces plot issues that didn’t previously exist. After confessing to attempting to sabotage the Games, Beetee is deemed too valuable to kill. That’s a stretch for a Snow who seems all too willing to kill over even perceived slights, especially since Beetee had already been caught plotting to sabotage the Capitol once before according to this film. It’s why they reaped his son. And he’s too valuable until, in Catching Fire, he suddenly isn’t, and is sent back into the arena.
Then there’s the footage. If the Capitol could manipulate Haymitch’s Games to make him look bad, why couldn’t they do the same to Katniss? Yes, her Games were live, but after a catastrophe like Haymitch’s, why would the Capitol ever run the Games truly live, rather than on a delay that only looks live? And why would they let Haymitch anywhere near Katniss — not once, but twice, including the Quarter Quell, which happens precisely because she’s become a problem?
Despite the comparisons some critics have made, this is not Andor. Sunrise on the Reaping is a well-meaning film that often defaults to fan service, such as with Fiennes’ Snow pausing dramatically to ask Plutarch if he’s ever considered a career in Gamemaking. Yes, we know that’s what he’ll do, but that question adds nothing to the world. The film drills home its themes through dialogue: Nothing is inevitable, each spark helps fuel the fire of rebellion, and quite literally, Haymitch’s stated goal of ending the Games. It’s far more telling than evoking, and adds no new layers to the franchise’s already well-worn themes.
Still, Sunrise on the Reaping has a worthy message. It’s true that the work of moving toward a world that reflects one’s values — whatever that looks like — is worthwhile in and of itself, whether or not it outwardly appears to succeed. And it’s fair to assume there was a silent underground well before the events of Catching Fire; the rebellion couldn’t have pulled off what it did otherwise. However, there were stronger ways for the franchise to get there.
Contrary to what some critics say, this world hasn’t necessarily run out of steam. The problem is that it keeps returning to the same story: a tribute from 12 in the arena — Katniss, Lucy Gray, now Haymitch. If the franchise wanted its own Andor, it could have been an extended series focused on the people working underground for decades to lay the groundwork for the rebellion we saw play out in Mockingjay. Imagine watching a true believer in Snow’s vision slowly become a rebel, set against the lives of ordinary citizens in the Capitol and the districts, including 13.
Collins has said she was inspired by Hume’s question of how easily the many are governed by the few, and in this film, Plutarch openly asks Haymitch why we submit. A series could actually dig into those ideas — privilege, media literacy, bias, the real power of propaganda — exploring how divisions are sown within a nation, and how the privileged, by nation and by class, are trained to dehumanize others. It would hold up a mirror to us all. Panem has more stories to tell, but the next one needs to be fresh — a tale that won’t undo the power of what’s come before… Haymitch’s hard-won redemption included.
